title: Incorporating environmental drivers and productivity changes into management strategy evaluation
content:
Abstract
Uncertainty in the effects of environmental changes on stock productivity remains a central problem and research priority for fisheries management. Management strategy evaluation (MSE) is increasingly advocated and used to simulation-test harvest strategies against environmental effects on productivity; however, the complexity of the data, models, and decisions entailed remain significant challenges for developers and practitioners. Moreover, practical guidance for conditioning and projecting environment–productivity relationships within MSE is still sparse. Based on the experiences of a diverse group of modelling experts, a generic workflow is devised and presented for developing and subsequently using environment–productivity relationships within single-species, nonspatial operating models (OMs) in MSE. In the first part, key data types, modelling objectives, and approaches for estimating and validating these relationships are described. Importantly, environment–productivity relationships should be based on clear hypotheses (potentially with stakeholder input), have covariates that match temporal and spatial scale of productivity processes, and have unexplained variability (i.e. process error) carefully scrutinized for patterns (e.g. nonstationarity) and projected accordingly. The second part of the paper identifies and describes methods for projecting environmental effects on productivity using climate models and without (i.e. altering productivity dynamics directly). Key tactical considerations are presented for designing OMs (e.g. include an OM with no climate forcing to benchmark results from OMs with forcing, devise edge cases for robustness) and evaluating management performance (e.g. define appropriate projection periods, consider dynamic reference points to calculate metrics). Despite the common use of single-species OMs, it is important to consider multispecies interactions, and fine-scale population and fishery dynamics, to better understand potential environmental effects on a target stock’s productivity. In summarizing key decision points and range of methods applied to date, this work serves to support informed choices and shared vocabulary for developing and conducting these MSEs, rather than a prescriptive checklist.
